blocks.text: Mercerus does not depart far from this interpretation; in his Commentary he renders these words: when even the locust shall be a burden to you, a very small creature, than which otherwise nothing is lighter. Among those who take חגב properly of the locust must also be counted Ludovicus de Dieu, who renders the Hebrew words וינאץ השקד ויסתבל החגב: although the almond tree blossoms, and the locust is laden with fat, i.e. although it is the most delightful season of the year, yet appetite will make it void (ותפר אביונה), and you will be able to derive no pleasure from it. Doederlein too, in his Scholia on the Poetical Books of the O. T. on this passage, p. 186, [III, 335] and in his German trans., thinks that the moroseness of old age is indicated by these words, although he renders the words themselves differently: the almond tree is despised (that tree is praised because it produces flowers and fruit early and before the others; as if to say, to old age even the joys of spring and of reviving nature are loathsome), and the locust makes itself troublesome; namely the locust, he says, which Anacreon also calls θέρεος προφήτης [thereos prophētēs], herald of summer, just as we noted above that the almond is put as a sign of the renewed year: this sign too, otherwise joyful, causes annoyance to the old man, who is dead to and hardened against the feeling of joys. Doederlein is followed by Io. Ern. Christ. Schmid in his German version of Ecclesiastes, entitled Salomo's Prediger, oder Koheleth's Lehren, Versuch einer neuen Uebersetzung und richtigern Erklärung, Giessen, 1794, p. 200, although in a note appended to that interpretation of the words יסתבל חגב he himself objects that it is very doubtful whether the Hebrew חגב is the same species of cicada as the Greek τεττιξ [tettix], to which they ascribe a λιγυρὴν οἴμην [ligyrēn oimēn]. But there is a weightier objection to Doederlein's interpretation: the chirping of the locust, a creature most hostile to the inhabitants of the Eastern lands, is nowhere for the poets of those peoples a herald of the most joyful season of the year, as it is for the Greek and Roman poets. This same point also tells against the opinion of Eusebius Traug. Ebert, who in his dissertation on this passage, entitled Imago Senis Salomonei ex Cap. XII. Ecclesiast., Leipzig 1770, renders our words: although the locust flits about, and the most beautiful season of the year begins. J. D. Michaelis, in the Programme written in the name of the Georgia Augusta Academy, by which the memory of Johann Matthias Gesner was commended to posterity, Göttingen, 1761 (which is inserted in the Syntagma Commentationum 2, Göttingen 1767), objects to the common interpretation, (remember your creator) until the locust becomes heavy, that it is ill suited to the nature of locusts and to the image of old age, since towards their old age locusts, which were previously bound to the earth, fly lightly through the air. He would therefore prefer, comparing the Arabic شبل [shabala], it grew, grew up, to render: before the locust grows up. For most kinds of locusts, he says, have a fivefold age: first true locusts, hopping and very small, break out of the eggs; then they shed their skin four times, and only after the fourth moult do they come forth winged, which is their fifth age. "As, then," Michaelis continues, "the locust through four ages either creeps or hops on the ground, a worm rather than a winged creature, and, having put off its skin for the fourth time, receives wings, and now nearer to heaven flies away, to seek an unknown shore beyond the sea: so we too throughout our whole life, divided into four ages, are bound to the earth; and when these are completed, and we are stripped of the body, we fly away to that homeland which the myths not only of the Greeks but also of the Orientals said lay beyond the vast sea, the islands of the blessed [see Michaelis, Epimetron added to Lowth's Ninth Lecture on the Sacred Poetry of the Hebrews, p. 195]. What, then, the psyche, that is the butterfly, was to the Greeks [an image of immortality, because, at first a worm bound to the earth and creeping on the ground, after a kind of sleep it would come forth winged and seek the heights; this image was richly illustrated by Io. Matth. Gesner in his Corollarium animarum Hippocratis, de illarum repraesentatione sub imagine papilionis; it is found in the Commentarii Societatis Regiae Scientiarum Goettingensis, vol. 1, p. 145 ff.], these winged locusts were to the East." Michaelis retained the same interpretation in the Supplemm. ad Lexx. Hebrr. vol. 3, p. 669 and vol. 5, p. 1711, but in such a way that in the former place he preferred to render יסתבל [III, 336] it is carried, i.e. it rises on high, it is lifted up; in the latter place, however, he returns to the notion of growing up. But rightly, in my judgement, Gottfr. Less, in the Vermischte Schriften vol. 1, p. 27 (in Essay 2, which bears the title Salomo verglichen mit Horaz [Ars poetica, vv. 169–174] und Cicero [Cato maior], vom weissen Genuss der Freuden des Lebens, nebst den zwey Gemählden des Greise-Alters und des Todes), objects to this interpretation that the usual meaning of the verb יסתבל does not fit this sense, and that it is not established from any other source that winged locusts were for the Hebrews, or for Orientals at all, an image of the passage of souls into the other life; moreover, the context of the whole discourse, which presents the troubles of advancing age in various images, stands against this interpretation. Less himself proposes two ways of interpreting: the reference is either to the hoarse voice of the cicada or to the various ages of that same creature. If the former, the words before the locust grows heavy are to be understood thus: before the voice becomes thin and fails. He prefers, however, the latter, so that חגב, the locust of the fourth age, is an image of the old man passing the last age of life, and יסתבל indicates either the failing of strength or the old man's back bent as if by a burden. But this whole interpretation rests on a very weak foundation, I might almost say on none at all, namely that חגב is the locust after its fourth moult. Much more uncertain still is the conjecture, also proposed by Less, that instead of החגב one should perhaps read ויסתבל החגם, before feasts are a burden, i.e. before one wearies of the pleasures and joys of this life. G. Zirkel, in the Untersuchungen über den Prediger, p. 361, renders our words the locust is carried, or when it is carried off, which he says happens when, having become fat and heavy, it is deprived of the power of flight and is caught and carried off by men; by this image he thinks advancing old age is described, when, as the strength of the body fails, the limbs move more slowly. A new interpretation was recently proposed by Henr. Frid. Pfannkuche in his Exercitationes in Ecclesiastae, Salomoni vulgo tributi, locum vexatissimum Cap. XI, 7.—XII, 7., Göttingen 1794. In this booklet he tried to show that that portion of Ecclesiastes contains not, as is commonly thought, a description of old age, but of every kind of misfortune and calamity, under the image of a storm with rains, gales and thunder, which is presented and variously embellished from verse 2 of Chapter XII onward. To this description of the storm also belongs, he says, the statement that small locusts (for he understands these by חגב, following Oedmann; see above, note 5 to Chapter I) are swept away by whirlwinds, or carried off; with the vowel points changed, of course, he reads יִסָּתֵבַל החגב, the locust is carried off, is swept away (by the winds, which are hostile to locusts). Whether this arbitrary change of reading, devised in favour of a hypothesis that is hardly firm, will win everyone's approval, we very much doubt.
